_fields.name: Stable identifier. What the study records and the API accepts.
_fields.label: Human-readable name, shown in the interface.
_fields.family: The ISLR family. The recommender reasons in families, so coverage matters more than count.
_fields.tasks: Which prediction types this method applies to. A method absent from a task is shown disabled with its reason, never hidden (FR-8.3).
_fields.needs_scaling: Whether the result depends on feature units. Distance-based, regularised and gradient-based methods do; trees do not.
_fields.handles_nan: Whether the method accepts missing values without imputation. Verified against the installed scikit-learn by the test suite, not merely declared.
_fields.tuning: `internal-cv` where the method has no meaningful default value and shipping it untuned would measure an arbitrary choice rather than the method (D-019).
_fields.implementation: `sklearn`, or `r` for the two methods whose reference implementations live there (D-020). The application offers both; only the backend differs.
_fields.rationale: What this method represents on the bias-variance and interpretability axes. The recommender's explanations are built from this.
_fields.incompatibility: Per task, why the method does not apply, in words a user without ML background can act on. Absent where the method applies.

_note: Generated by scripts/export_methods.py from the registry in src/mlsandbox/methods.py. Do not edit by hand: the study and the application read the same table so they cannot disagree about which methods exist.

methods.name: linear_regression
methods.label: Linear Regression
methods.rationale: The high-bias, fully interpretable baseline every other method is judged against.

incompatibility.classification: Linear Regression predicts continuous numbers, and your target is categories.

methods.name: logistic_regression
methods.label: Logistic Regression
methods.rationale: The interpretable classification baseline: coefficients read as log-odds.

incompatibility.regression: Logistic Regression predicts categories, and your target is a continuous number.

methods.name: ridge
methods.label: Ridge
methods.rationale: Shrinks coefficients without eliminating them. Where correlated predictors would make plain linear regression unstable.

methods.name: lasso
methods.label: Lasso
methods.rationale: Drives coefficients to exactly zero, so it selects features as well as fits. Its appeal is interpretability under high dimensionality.

methods.name: knn
methods.label: K-Nearest Neighbours
methods.rationale: Assumes nothing about the shape of the relationship, and pays for it in high dimensions, where every point is far from every other.

methods.name: lda
methods.label: Linear Discriminant Analysis
methods.rationale: Stable where logistic regression struggles: small samples, well-separated classes.

incompatibility.regression: Linear Discriminant Analysis predicts categories, and your target is a continuous number.

methods.name: qda
methods.label: Quadratic Discriminant Analysis
methods.rationale: Allows each class its own covariance, buying a curved boundary at the price of many more parameters.

incompatibility.regression: Quadratic Discriminant Analysis predicts categories, and your target is a continuous number.

methods.name: naive_bayes
methods.label: Naive Bayes
methods.rationale: Assumes features are independent, which is almost never true and often works anyway. Very high bias, very cheap.

incompatibility.regression: Naive Bayes predicts categories, and your target is a continuous number.

methods.name: pcr
methods.label: Principal Components Regression
methods.rationale: Compresses correlated predictors before fitting. Components are chosen without reference to the target, which is its weakness against PLS.

incompatibility.classification: Principal Components Regression predicts continuous numbers, and your target is categories.

methods.name: pls
methods.label: Partial Least Squares
methods.rationale: Like PCR, but builds components that relate to the target.

incompatibility.classification: Partial Least Squares predicts continuous numbers, and your target is categories.

methods.name: polynomial
methods.label: Polynomial Regression
methods.rationale: The simplest way out of linearity, and the least controlled: high degrees oscillate wildly at the edges of the data.

incompatibility.classification: Polynomial Regression predicts continuous numbers, and your target is categories.

methods.name: splines
methods.label: Regression Splines
methods.rationale: Local flexibility without the edge behaviour of high-degree polynomials.

incompatibility.classification: Regression Splines predicts continuous numbers, and your target is categories.

methods.name: decision_tree
methods.label: Decision Tree
methods.rationale: The most interpretable non-linear method: the model is a diagram someone can read. Unstable — small data changes redraw it.

methods.name: bagging
methods.label: Bagging
methods.rationale: Averages many trees to cure a single tree's instability, at the cost of the diagram.

methods.name: random_forest
methods.label: Random Forest
methods.rationale: Bagging plus decorrelated trees. The strong default when interpretability is not required.

methods.name: boosting
methods.label: Gradient Boosting
methods.rationale: Fits trees sequentially to what the previous ones got wrong. Often the accuracy ceiling on tabular data (D-023: histogram implementation).

methods.name: svm_linear
methods.label: Support Vector Classifier
methods.rationale: A linear boundary chosen to maximise the margin. Robust in high dimensions.

methods.name: svm_rbf
methods.label: Support Vector Machine (RBF)
methods.rationale: A curved boundary via the kernel trick. Scales badly: cost grows roughly with the square of the sample size.

methods.name: mlp
methods.label: Neural Network (MLP)
methods.rationale: Maximum flexibility, minimum interpretability, and hungry for data — the far end of the spectrum the recommender reasons about.

methods.name: gam
methods.label: Generalised Additive Model
methods.rationale: Flexible per feature while staying additive, so each variable's effect remains readable. Runs through R's mgcv, whose implementation is the reference (D-020).

methods.name: bart
methods.label: BART
methods.rationale: Bayesian tree ensemble, giving uncertainty intervals rather than point predictions. Runs through R's dbarts: Python has no solid implementation (D-020).
